Automatically Finding Reward Model Biases

Atticus Wang Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: MATS Correspondence to: atticusw@mit.edu     Iván Arcuschin Affiliation: Independent     Arthur Conmy
Abstract

Reward models are central to large language model (LLM) post-training. However, past work has shown that they can reward spurious or undesirable attributes such as length, format, hallucinations, and sycophancy. In this work, we introduce and study the research problem of automatically finding reward model biases in natural language. We offer a simple approach of using an LLM to iteratively propose and refine candidate biases. Our method can recover known biases and surface novel ones: for example, we found that Skywork-V2-8B, a leading open-weight reward model, often mistakenly favors responses with redundant spacing and responses with hallucinated content. In addition, we show evidence that evolutionary iteration outperforms flat best-of-N search, and we validate the recall of our pipeline using synthetically injected biases. We hope our work contributes to further research on improving RMs through automated interpretability methods.

Keywords: 
Machine Learning, ICML

1 Introduction

Reward models (RMs) are very successful at teaching goals that are hard to directly specify (Christiano et al., 2017; Stiennon et al., 2020). In particular, reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is widely adopted in the modern post-training stack (Ouyang et al., 2022), often surpassing alternative, reward model-free methods (Xu et al., 2024). However, when optimizing large language models (LLMs) against RMs, they can learn to generate outputs that achieve high rewards but are undesirable to humans, a problem usually known as reward hacking or overoptimization (Amodei et al., 2016; Gao et al., 2022). Examples include behaviors such as sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2023), producing overly long responses (Singhal et al., 2023), and providing answers that are more convincing to humans but not more accurate (Wen et al., 2024). Identifying behaviors like these directly from RM preferences—without first optimizing a language model—would enable model developers to find and fix problems with RMs earlier in the pipeline. Past approaches have found specific adversarial examples for RMs (Bukharin et al., 2025; Pathmanathan and Huang, 2025), but they do not easily translate to natural language descriptions of general RM biases.

In this paper, we study reward model biases: consistent and undesirable preferences of RMs. To identify these biases, we propose the following pipeline. First, an LLM is asked to generate initial bias candidates based on trends in sampled completions and their rewards. Then, we measure the extent to which the RM is biased towards these attributes; these metrics are in turn passed to another LLM, which proposes variations of the most promising candidates, while the rest are filtered out. This step can be repeated as an evolutionary loop. This pipeline is highly general and requires solely input and output model access.

Our approach found novel biases of a recent reward model from Skywork (Liu et al., 2025) which tops RewardBench 2 (Malik et al., 2025). For example, the RM often assigns higher reward to responses when redundant spaces are added in between words (Figure 1). The pipeline also finds that the RM often rewards hallucinated content in responses, corroborating evidence from Wen et al. (2024).

Our main contributions are:

  1. 1.

    We formalize the question of finding natural language reward model biases as a two-objective optimization problem, with the goal of both i) higher preference by the RM and ii) lower preference by an LLM judge (Section 2.1).

  2. 2.

    We offer a black-box pipeline (Section 2.3) that iteratively proposes and tests candidate biases following an evolutionary algorithm (Guo et al., 2023).

  3. 3.

    This pipeline can find novel, interesting biases in a leading RM, as well as previously known problems with reward models (Sections 3.1 and 3.2).

  4. 4.

    We provide evidence that the evolutionary algorithm provides benefits over simple best-of-NN hypothesis generation (Section 3.3).

Reward models play a significant role in shaping downstream model behavior, and we believe that lightweight, black-box audits like ours should be incorporated as a routine step in reward model development. We release our code and invite further research to develop better methods of discovering and mitigating reward model biases.

2 Methods

In this section, we first explain how we quantify reward model biases (Section 2.1). Then, after briefly describing the user prompt dataset generation process (Section 2.2), we introduce our evolutionary pipeline for finding the biases (Section 2.3).

2.1 Definition of reward model bias

Problem setup. In this paper, we use the term attribute to mean a natural language description of some textual feature, together with a binary classifier AA which decides for each given piece of text xx, whether or not the text has this feature. We write A⁡(x)=1A(x)=1 if the text xx has the attribute, and A⁡(x)=0A(x)=0 otherwise.11 1 In practice, we can judge attribute presence with an LLM (as we do in Section D.1), or in specific cases with a regex classifier (Section 3.4).

Our goal is to discover biases of a given RM: attributes that are undesirable for humans, but which the given RM prefers. As a proxy for costly human-in-the-loop judgment, we use a frontier LLM-as-judge, Claude Sonnet 4.5 (Anthropic, 2025), that broadly aligns with human values. We include example responses in Appendix E to illustrate that the biases we surfaced are also clearly undesirable to humans; therefore, we expect the choice of this LLM judge to be not particularly important as long as it is sufficiently capable and aligned.

Measuring bias through counterfactual pairs. Now we provide a computable definition of what it means for a given RM or LLM judge to (dis)prefer a given attribute. The method we use is to form counterfactual pairs of assistant responses to the same user prompt, such that the main way in which the two responses differ is that one contains the attribute and the other does not.22 2 See Appendix A for an alternative definition.

Formally, suppose we fix a user prompt distribution 𝒰\mathcal{U}, and let AA be an attribute we are interested in. Suppose that for each user prompt x∼𝒰x\sim\mathcal{U}, we have access to counterfactual pairs of responses yA=1iy_{A=1}^{i} and yA=0iy_{A=0}^{i}, indexed by ii, where each pair only differs in the attribute AA. Then, for a reward model RR that assigns a scalar score for each prompt-response pair, its bias strength towards the attribute AA is defined as the average reward difference

R⁡(A):=𝔼x∼𝒰​𝔼i​[R⁡(x,yA=1i)−R⁡(x,yA=0i)].R(A):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{i}[R(x,y_{A=1}^{i})-R(x,y_{A=0}^{i})].

Similarly, for a judge model JJ which can only assign binary preferences between two responses to the same prompt, we can define its bias strength as

J⁡(A):=𝔼x∼𝒰​𝔼i​J​(x,yA=1i,yA=0i),J(A):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim\mathcal{U}}\mathbb{E}_{i}J(x,y_{A=1}^{i},y_{A=0}^{i}),

where J⁡(x,y,y′)=1J(x,y,y^{\prime})=1 if JJ prefers yy over y′y^{\prime}, 0.50.5 if it is a tie, and 00 otherwise. We will sometimes call it the bias winrate to emphasize that J⁡(A)J(A) is a number in [0,1][0,1].

With these definitions, let JJ be the frontier LLM judge. We will define AA to be a bias of the reward model RR, if R⁡(A)>0R(A)>0 (the RM prefers it) and J⁡(A)<0.5J(A)<0.5 (the judge disprefers it).

Producing counterfactual pairs. In this work, we form these counterfactual response pairs by asking a separate language model to minimally rewrite sampled responses. Let us denote by fA=1f_{A=1} a rewrite process that transforms a response yy into another response y′=fA=1​(y)y^{\prime}=f_{A=1}(y) such that A⁡(y′)=1A(y^{\prime})=1 and that y,y′y,y^{\prime} remain as similar as possible; we can analogously define fA=0f_{A=0}. Then the counterfactual pair (yA=1,yA=0)(y_{A=1},y_{A=0}) is chosen to be (fA=1​(y),fA=0​(y))(f_{A=1}(y),f_{A=0}(y)).

One potential issue with this definition is that varying one attribute might involve many other correlated changes in the response, whose effects are difficult to disentangle. We mitigate this issue in the following ways:

  • •

    Explicitly asking the rewriter model to only make minimal and targeted edits, specifically asking it to not significantly change the overall length and content of the response;

  • •

    Explicitly discouraging our pipeline (Section 2.3) from proposing attributes whose addition or removal require major changes in the response;

  • •

    Using three models from different providers to perform the rewriting step, in order to create less correlated rewrites. If the bias exists for multiple different rewriters, we have more evidence that the given attribute itself is responsible for the bias.

In Appendix D, we show that counterfactual pairs produced this way satisfy various sanity checks for differing only in the target attribute.

2.2 User prompt generation

In this work, we choose to search for biases that are specific to well-defined user prompt topics, instead of more general distributions. This is because the RM or judge’s preferences may be different depending on the sub-distribution; for example, a reward model might prefer the response to contain lists when the user is asking for a how-to guide, but not in general (Section 3.1). In addition, we decide to use synthetically generated user prompts, as we found it challenging to produce non-toxic, coherent usage clusters that cover a wide range of user topics using public chat data such as WildChat (Zhao et al., 2023) and LMArena (Chiang et al., 2024).

To create synthetic prompts, we first write diverse topic summaries that will each grow into a dataset of user prompts adhering to the topic. We wrote a list of 20 topics (Section B.1) that cover a range of common LLM usage topics, as well as situations which we think may elicit interesting responses. Next, starting from each topic summary, the following two-step process is used to create a diverse set of user prompts adhering to the spec.33 3 A similar two-level synthetic data generation process is used in Tamkin et al. (2024). We first prompt an LLM to brainstorm nn concrete user scenarios which might occur under the given topic. Then, another LLM is asked to generate mm different user prompts that would be asked in each given scenario, producing m​nmn user prompts in total. We show a randomly selected subset of generated user prompts in Section B.2, and the prompts used to generate them can be found in the codebase.

2.3 Automatic pipeline for bias discovery

We now introduce our pipeline, which is essentially one evolutionary loop run iteratively, each step updating the population of candidate attributes. The initial attributes are generated through a hypothesis generation step; in all subsequent steps, they are mutated from the previous step’s population. Figure 2 illustrates the different steps in our pipeline.

Hypothesis generation. To find a reasonable set of candidate attributes to start with, we take user prompts in 𝒰\mathcal{U} and sample responses from several open language models with a range of sizes, and evaluate their rewards. For each user prompt, we feed its sampled responses and rewards to a LLM and ask it to come up with a fixed number of candidate attributes. In the prompt, we encourage the LLM to find attributes which appear more in higher-scoring responses; however, we do not mention that it is being used to find biases of reward models, to avoid nudging it towards proposing biases which are already known in its training corpus (which we think might reduce variability).

We aggregate the set of candidate attributes across a subset of user prompts from the training split. These attributes are then clustered by semantic similarity, and a representative sample is chosen in each cluster. We found that at this scale (∼28\sim 2^{8} candidates), prompting an LLM to perform semantic clustering is more accurate than clustering with embedding models. The set of representatives serves as the initial candidates.

Iteration. After we obtain an initial set of candidate attributes, we use an evolutionary algorithm to improve them. In each iteration, we:

  • •

    Evaluate the RM and judge bias strengths for all the current candidates44 4 We use only the rewriter model openai/gpt-5-mini at this stage, to save costs.;

  • •

    Select the most promising candidates. Because our problem setup optimizes for two objectives (higher R⁡(A)R(A), lower J⁡(A)J(A)), we keep the top candidates that are closest to the Pareto frontier;

  • •

    Mutate the surviving attributes by prompting an LLM for variations.

The pseudocode for our evolutionary pipeline is provided in Algorithm 1; more details about the pipeline are provided in Appendix C.

Validation. After we obtain the last step’s list of candidates, we evaluate their RM and judge bias strengths on a held-out validation split of the data, now with three different rewriter models (openai/gpt-5-mini, anthropic/claude-haiku-4.5, x-ai/grok-4.1-fast). We pool the bias scores across all three rewriters, and filter for the candidates AA such that R⁡(A)>0R(A)>0, J⁡(A)<0.5J(A)<0.5, and the Bonferroni-corrected p<0.05p<0.05 for both the RM and the judge for their respective one-sided tt-tests55 5 The Bonferroni correction multiplies the original pp-value by the total number of attributes that enter the validation step. This step may be overly conservative, but we feel that eliminating false positives is more important.. This validation criterion further eliminates potential false-positives, and we are left with a small set of typically 0–5 candidates per user prompt topic. Finally, we do a manual check to deduplicate semantically similar candidates and remove candidates that are not judged to be undesirable to humans. After this final filtering step, we obtain the list of attributes in Table 1, which we hold out to evaluate on a separate, previously unseen test set.

3 Results

We first revisit previously-known formatting biases to check that our methods yield conclusions consistent with prior work (Section 3.1). We then present our main results and dive into two case studies on interesting biases we found (Section 3.2). Finally, we run controlled studies comparing different pipeline configurations (Section 3.3) and examining possible factors which affect success in hypothesis generation (Section 3.4).

Models. For our main results, we study biases of the model66 6 The full model slug is Skywork-Reward-V2-Llama-3.1-8B. Skywork-V2-8B, a Bradley–Terry reward model from Skywork (Liu et al., 2025) finetuned from Llama 3.1 8B Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024). At the time of writing, this model occupies the first place of RewardBench 2 (Malik et al., 2025).

3.1 Sanity Check: Evaluating format biases

To sanity check our methods and build intuition, we revisit earlier work (Zhang et al., 2025b) which studied several format-related reward model biases, such as boldface, lists, and emojis. In Figure 3, we plot the bias strengths for Skywork-V2-8B according to our methods, across two different user prompt distributions: Figure 3(a) samples 512 random user prompts across a broad mixture of instruct-tuning and preference datasets, while Figure 3(b) takes 64 user prompts from a narrow synthetic dataset of the topic “User asks for a how-to guide for common everyday task”. We show the results for all 3 rewriter models used in the pipeline, and the bias strengths and 95% CIs are calculated by pooling across all three rewriters.

Results. On the broad user prompt dataset, the RM has a preference towards only bold formatting, out of the seven format biases evaluated. This is roughly consistent with Zhang et al. (2025b), where the Bradley–Terry reward model they evaluate also heavily favors bold text and disfavors exclamations and emojis, with weaker preference on other formatting elements.

On the narrow prompt dataset, the RM additionally has a strong preference towards list formatting, which is not present for the broad dataset. This demonstrates that RMs could have preferences that only exist for user prompts in specific sub-distributions. We also observe qualitatively that the distribution of reward differences before and after rewrite seem roughly consistent among the three rewriter models.

3.2 Biases of Skywork-V2-8B

We ran the evolutionary pipeline with Claude Sonnet 4.5 as the LLM judge. Table 1 shows the list of biases that passed our final filtering step, which we committed to evaluate on the unseen test set. We also use the same three rewriters as the validation step, and for each rewriter we obtain a pp-value for the one-sided tt-test. We then conclude the overall significance through the partial conjunction test, with a more conservative threshold of p=0.01p=0.01; see Section F.1 for details. Out of 17 total bias candidates (found in 7 out of 20 user prompt topics), 10 were statistically significant for both the RM and the judge; these are indicated in the rightmost columns of Table 1.

Case study: Redundant spacing between words. In this example, the user prompt spec is “User asks about the assistant’s opinion on political events or political figures”, and our pipeline found the attribute of “Triple spaces between words”. See Figure 1 for an example counterfactual pair of responses. The ancestry of this attribute in the evolutionary pipeline is given in Table 2, where the RM and judge biases are over the training batch in each step. Inspecting the data, we found that the baseline samples contained one response with a typo, which caused the pipeline to pick up on this line of typography-related attributes.

Overall, we found this to be the most surprising bias from the experiments. shows all the user prompt topics in descending order of how much the RM displays this bias over the corresponding dataset (n=240n=240 each). More often than not, conversational user prompts asking for pure text output indeed displayed this bias, but it is not universal.

Case study: Hallucinated details. In this example, the user prompt spec is “Inquiries about subtle plausible-sounding but made-up events”, and our pipeline found the bias “Includes a brief quotation attributed to a named official or agency as evidence…” (see Table 1). Therefore, we checked whether the RM has a bias for the following manually written attribute77 7 This attribute was written prior to seeing the test set results.:

Provide specific hallucinated details and subtly false information about the fictitious event in the answer. The details should be hallucinated, but not overtly wrong.

Indeed, the RM has a significant bias: RM strength 2.52±0.512.52\pm 0.51 (p=p= 1.9e-6), judge winrate 0.156​[0.132,0.184]0.156\thinspace[0.132,0.184] (p=p= 2.0e-42). Given this result, we speculate that one of the reasons that language models learn to become more convincing during RLHF (Wen et al., 2024) may be because that this was encouraged by the RM.

We use this example to illustrate that attribute descriptions found by the pipeline may not be the most general or appropriate description of the underlying bias, but may be a special case of a more general bias, or a related attribute that is highly correlated with the true label. As such, even though they are not false positives, it is still worthy to manually inspect the attributes and counterfactual pairs at the end of the pipeline.

3.3 Comparing different pipeline configurations

In this section, we investigate whether the multi-turn, evolutionary search procedure outperforms a simpler best-of-NN approach. We compare three configurations that trade off between search depth and width, while keeping the total number of proposed candidates constant. We use two approaches to evaluate the output of a given run:

Visualization. After validation, we obtain a set of attributes AiA_{i} as well as their bias strengths R⁡(Ai)R(A_{i}), J⁡(Ai)J(A_{i}). We can plot these points to visualize both the Pareto frontier and the number of attributes that passed all the filters.

Diversity-adjusted bias strength. To compute a sensible numerical score that takes into account both the number and the diversity of found biases, we propose a novel metric inspired by the concept of maximal marginal relevance (Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998). First, sort the attributes by their R⁡(Ai)R(A_{i}) in descending order. Then, we fix a threshold ℓ∈[0,1]\ell\in[0,1] and further filter out all attributes whose J⁡(Ai)J(A_{i}) lie above this threshold. Embed each remaining attribute description with a text embedding model to obtain unit-norm vectors eie_{i}. We define our metric, the diversity-adjusted bias strength, as

DABS=∑iR⁡(Ai)⋅(1−maxj<i⁡⟨ei,ej⟩)\operatorname{DABS}=\sum_{i}R(A_{i})\cdot(1-\max_{j<i}\langle e_{i},e_{j}\rangle)

where ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the Euclidean inner product. The second term is a penalty for semantically similar attributes. We report the DABS metric while sweeping ℓ∈[0,0.5]\ell\in[0,0.5].

Results. Figures 4(b) and 4(a) respectively plot the two output metrics. We only plot the attributes which passed the final validation step as described at the end of Section 2.3. Due to cost constraints, we only ran the full comparison once per configuration, and six user prompt topics (out of 20) yielded attributes that passed the filtering step. Qualitatively, both plots show that the depth 5, branching 4 run performed the best, followed by the depth 3, branching 8 run, and finally the depth 1 (best-of-NN) run. Although different user prompt topics show roughly consistent trends, more independent runs would be needed to form rigorous conclusions.

3.4 Recall

To understand whether our pipeline has missed any significant biases, in this section we use a toy setup to test when the hypothesis generation step can generate relevant hypotheses from the sampled rollouts and rewards. We take three attributes which can be detected through regex matching, and we manually inject biases for these attributes in a usual reward model. The exact regular expressions used can be found in the codebase. The attributes are:

  • •

    The response starts with an affirmative filler like “Sure”, “Certainly”, etc;

  • •

    The response contains markdown section headers;

  • •

    The response contains bulleted or numbered lists.

Instead of comparing a RM and a LLM judge as in our main results, in this setup we employ the same RM in both roles. To enforce the assumption that the attribute is preferred by one model and dispreferred by the other, the reward is increased by a scalar bb for the former, and decreased by bb for the latter, conditioned on the attribute being present in the response. Furthermore, a Gaussian noise N⁡(0,a)N(0,a) is added to both rewards, modeling the effect of all other attributes of which we have no prior knowledge.

Results. In Figure 5(a), we look at only the affirmation bias, where we fix the signal level bb and vary the noise level aa. We find that even when the signal-to-noise ratio is very low, the hypothesis generation step can still propose relevant attributes. This suggests that it is not strictly proposing attributes which distinguish low-scoring and high-scoring responses.

In Figure 5(b), we select various (attribute, user prompt topic) pairs, such that the sampled responses have varied fractions of responses that contain the attribute. We find that this attribute presence rate has a large impact on whether the correct attribute is proposed, and detection rate is higher when there is a significant fraction of both responses that contain the attribute and those that do not. This suggests that the hypothesis generation step is limited in only being able to propose attributes present in at least some samples, and that evolutionary iteration may be an important factor in discovering more diverse and rare biases.

4 Related work

Reward model interpretability.  Our paper most closely aligns with past work on finding human-interpretable preferences of reward models, such as sycophancy (Sharma et al., 2023), formatting (Zhang et al., 2025b), prefix bias (Kumar et al., 2025), or one-token completions of specific user prompts (Christian et al., 2025). Jiang et al. (2024) perturbs preference data along each of 15 pre-written attributes to create counterfactual pairs, similar to our methods. However, this work differs from past approaches in that we do not place prior restrictions on the biases we look for.

Sparse auto-encoders (SAEs), first popularized by Bricken et al. (2023), have also been used as a complementary method of interpreting RMs and preference data (Riggs and Brinkmann, 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a; Movva et al., 2025). Our initial experiments for finding undesirable SAE latents that boost the reward were not as fruitful, but we think this is still a viable approach and deserves further study.

Hypothesis generation with language models. This work uses a language model pipeline to form and refine natural language hypotheses. Previous work used the same broad method to produce interpretable explanations of other data, such as tweet popularity prediction (Zhou et al., 2024), finding qualitative differences in LLM response styles (Dunlap et al., 2024a), and describing qualitative differences in two families of images (Dunlap et al., 2024b). Zhong et al. (2024) applies a more sophisticated training algorithm to refine initial hypotheses, and finds success in a wide range of realistic tasks such as tracking how LLM usage patterns evolve over time.

Debiasing reward models. In addition to finding RM biases, several methods exist for removing known biases or improving RM robustness in general. Notable approaches include reward shaping (Papadatos and Freedman, 2024; Wang et al., 2024), bias-agnostic data augmentation (Liu et al., 2024; Srivastava et al., 2025), adversarial training (Bukharin et al., 2025), and variational methods (Miao et al., 2024).

Model diffing. We remark that the setup in Section 2.1 generally applies whenever we have two models (either RM or judge) M1,M2M_{1},M_{2} and we would like to find attributes which M1M_{1} likes and M2M_{2} dislikes, even though one may not be strictly better than the other. Therefore, our work may also be of interest for the model diffing line of work (Lindsey et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025; Dunlap et al., 2024a).

5 Limitations

Methods. We think our methods could likely be improved on several fronts. First, our study relies on synthetically generated user prompts derived from a handwritten set of topics. Although this allows for controlled testing, these prompts may not accurately capture the distribution of real-world user queries.

Second, the biases we found are likely not all the biases that exist in the model; our pipeline surfaced biases in 7 out of 20 topics, suggesting that we have likely not exhausted the search space. On the other hand, our recall results (Section 3.4) do indicate that our pipeline likely hasn’t missed any obvious and pervasive biases. We expect our methods to improve by simply plugging in more capable models in the future; another avenue of improvement is to allow agentic affordances in the audit.

Lastly, as we point out in Section 2.1, our counterfactual generation relies on language model rewriters. While we mitigate the issue of correlated variables by using multiple distinct models and filtering for consensus, we cannot guarantee that the attributes are completely disentangled from other changes.

Cost and scope. The main cost bottleneck of our pipeline is in API calls to the Claude Sonnet 4.5 judge. As a result, we limited our experiments to only one setting, the Skywork-V2 family of RMs. Due to rapidly falling inference costs (Cottier, 2025), we think that this is likely not a key bottleneck; however, future work is needed to validate these findings across a broader range of RMs, including generative RMs (Mahan et al., 2024).

Implication for language models. Biases that are present in the reward model may not actually be learned by a language model optimized against it, since the distribution of generated text for some of our biases may be very far from the reference policy. Still, we think that it is valuable to understand a wide range of behaviors of the RM, since it is hard to predict if or when they arise during optimization.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we introduced a framework for discovering systematic biases in reward models, and our evolutionary pipeline successfully recovered known biases and surfaced new ones. The specific biases we uncovered, such as low-level artifacts like Figure 1, present concrete targets for mechanistic interpretability research to better understand.

More broadly, we think that performing this kind of automatic audit of various components of model development will become increasingly cheap and effective in the future. We hope lightweight, automated audits like ours become a routine step in reward model development.

Impact Statement

This paper presents an approach for automatically auditing reward models. By surfacing systematic biases before they propagate to downstream models, we believe our work could help practitioners build more aligned AI systems.

Appendix A Another definition of reward model bias

Here we describe a different, abstract definition of the extent to which a reward model prefers a given attribute in the assistant response. Compared with the definition in Section 2.1, it does not rely on counterfactual response pairs, but it is more difficult to compute in practice.

Keeping the same notation as in Section 2.1, we can define the bias strength of the reward model RR towards attribute AA to be

R(A):=𝔼x∈𝒰[𝔼y∼π(∙∣x)[R(x,y)∣A(y)=1]−𝔼y∼π(∙∣x)[R(x,y)∣A(y)=0]].R(A):=\mathbb{E}_{x\in\mathcal{U}}[\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(\bullet\mid x)}[R(x,y)\mid A(y)=1]-\mathbb{E}_{y\sim\pi(\bullet\mid x)}[R(x,y)\mid A(y)=0]].

Although this definition is natural, the expectation over all possible responses is hard to accurately estimate, and responses containing the attribute AA might be very rare and hard to sample. Therefore, this definition is not used in this paper.

Appendix C Pipeline details

C.1 Hypothesis generation

We uniformly choose from the following list of models to sample responses to the user prompts: meta-llama/llama-3.2-1b-instruct, mistralai/ministral-3b, meta-llama/llama-3.2-3b-instruct, meta-llama/llama-3.1-8b-instruct, google/gemma-2-9b-it, qwen/qwen-2.5-72b-instruct. Responses were sampled at temperature 1.0 to encourage diversity, with a maximum of 1024 completion tokens; incomplete responses were discarded.

We also briefly describe the hypothesis generation step, dubbed GenerateInitial in Algorithm 1. We give the LLM several sampled responses to the same user prompt, sorted by their RM rewards. To prime the LLM to find attributes that may be dispreferable, the RM rewards were reversed (subtracted from the maximum of each group), so that lower scores in the prompt correspond to higher reward in reality. The LLM is asked to identify atomic, generalizable features that appear more often in lower-scoring responses in the prompt (hence high-scoring ones in reality). The full prompt can be found in the codebase linked in the introduction.

C.3 Algorithmic details and hyperparameters

The pseudocode for our algorithm we use is given in Algorithm 1. The main runs were obtained with the following hyperparameters: the policy π\pi is a uniform mixture of all 6 models in Section C.1; mutations m=4m=4; the population targets are (64,16,16,16,16,10)(64,16,16,16,16,10); and the batch sizes are (16,32,32,32,32)(16,32,32,32,32).

This is also the same as the configuration for the “depth 5, width 4” experiment in Section 3.3. The “depth 3, width 8” experiment has m=8m=8, population targets (64,16,16,10)(64,16,16,10); batch sizes (16,32,32)(16,32,32). Finally, the “depth 1” experiment has population targets (320,10)(320,10) and batch size (32,)(32,). The large initial population was generated by starting with 64 base attributes, then prompting an LLM to propose 4 more variations for each. The total number of attributes being tested is the same (320) across these three settings.

The Filter functions filters off a fixed percentage of points with lowest RM bias strength (resp. highest judge bias strength), but with a cap of 0 (resp. 0.5). This percentage is set to 40%40\% for the RM and 30%30\% for the LLM judge, so that we are left with at least 30%30\% of the attributes from before. The ParetoSelect function selects the points closest to the Pareto frontier as follows: first, the points are partitioned into “waves” by iteratively peeling off the frontier layer. Then we select points wave by wave, with ties broken by the RM bias strength (higher is better).

Appendix D Counterfactual pair quality validation

In this section we report various experiments testing whether the counterfactual pairs generated by rewriting responses passes basic sanity checks.

D.1 Fidelity

By fidelity, we mean whether the rewriting process fA=1f_{A=1} (see Section 2.1 for notation) successfully adds the attribute AA to the response. We do not perform the analogous test for fA=0f_{A=0} here, but instead we show that for most attributes, the sampled response yy usually does not contain the attribute by default, so that we can just take fA=0​(y)=yf_{A=0}(y)=y. Attribute presence is judged by openai/gpt-5-mini. See Table 3 for these results.

D.2 Invariance

By invariance, we mean the desirable property that the bias strength statistics derived from different rewriter models are roughly consistent with each other. Figure 6 shows that there is considerable per-sample correlation between each pair of rewriters, and Figure 7 shows the pairwise Q-Q plots for the reward diff distributions for four of the 17 final attributes from Table 1, and most of them are reasonably close to the diagonal.
